documents.title: Generative AI Syllabus Statement Considerations
tiers: No use of generative AI permitted
Use permitted under some circumstances or with explicit permission
documents.summary: CTE guidance offering three institutional options for AI syllabus statements and recommending a hybrid: a minimum-syllabus addition requiring instructors and students to set expectations and tying AI use to the Aggie Honor Code. Most of the text is sample statements from other universities, grouped into three permission levels.
documents.stance_why: The document sets no single rule. It recommends a hybrid in which instructors and students "establish clear expectations for generative AI use within each course and/or assignment", and its samples come in three permission-level tiers that are "not institutional policies", so the stance is delegates.

units.why: The document organizes sample statements into three permission levels (no use; some circumstances or explicit permission; broader use within guidelines), i.e. named tiers of AI use, so P05.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (actor: A=admin, B=instructor; phase: A=before-course, B=course-start). Source: the heading 'Sample Syllabus Statements Grouped by Permission Level' introduces the three-tier structure the guidance offers. The tiers are published by the university office for instructors to adopt, so actor admin and phase before-course (A) fit; B's instructor/course-start describes who uses the samples later.
units.anchor: Sample Syllabus Statements Grouped by Permission Level

units.why: The opening sentence says the university wishes to approach generative AI "with scholarly rigor, intellectual integrity, and educational excellence"; it sets institution-wide purpose and principles, so P56, informs, general.
units.anchor: with scholarly rigor, intellectual integrity, and educational excellence

units.why: Says AI brings "additional challenges to academic integrity" and "stimulating opportunities to educate effectively for the future of learning and work"; the work-preparation half is P44, and the integrity half is in fit_note.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=neutral, B=encourage). Source: 'The university recognizes that generative AI presents additional challenges to academic integrity and simultaneously presents stimulating opportunities'. It names both risk and opportunity, so it is a balanced rationale, not an endorsement; unit_stance is neutral. B's anchor is kept because it carries both halves of the sentence.
units.anchor: The university recognizes that generative AI presents additional challenges to academic integrity and simultaneously presents
units.fit_note: Also names academic-integrity challenges; the unit is a balanced rationale. | Also names academic-integrity challenges, not only opportunities.

units.why: The recommended course of action pairs a university-level syllabus requirement with individual instructor determinations (option 2: "allow individual instructors to determine their own syllabus statement"); this assigns the decision on acceptable use to instructors, so P04.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. Source: '(Recommended) Pursue a hybrid of the two previous options'. It is the document's recommended course of action, so it is a recommendation (should) to the institution: kept. B coded the optional options 1 and 2 instead (dropped) and did not code the recommendation itself.
units.anchor: (Recommended) Pursue a hybrid of the two previous options
units.policy: The recommended approach for the institution is a hybrid of a university-wide minimum syllabus requirement and individual instructors determining acceptable generative AI use in their own courses.
units.fit_note: Hybrid: university sets a minimum syllabus requirement and instructors decide the actual rule.

units.why: The recommended option adds a minimum syllabus requirement that makes explicit the "responsibility of instructors and students to establish clear expectations" in each course or assignment; this is the syllabus-statement requirement (P09), not P04 because it mandates stating expectations.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (actor: A=admin, B=all; phase: A=before-course, B=course-start). Source: the recommended hybrid 'makes explicit the responsibility of instructors and students to establish clear expectations'. The requirement is a university-level addition to the minimum syllabus requirements, so the actor is admin and the phase is before-course (institutional set-up), as A said; B's reading (all, course-start) describes who later acts on it, not who is bound by this sentence.
units.anchor: responsibility of instructors and students to establish clear expectations for generative AI use
units.policy: The recommended hybrid adds a minimum syllabus requirement making explicit the responsibility of instructors and students to establish clear expectations for generative AI use within each course and/or assignment.

units.why: The syllabus requirement "reinforces that the use of generative AI in academic coursework is integrally related to academic integrity and will be governed by the Aggie Honor Code"; this classifies AI use under the integrity code (P36).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (actor: A=admin, B=all; modality: A=must, B=informs; unit_stance: A=restrict, B=neutral). Source: the hybrid addition 'reinforces that the use of generative AI in academic coursework is integrally related to academic integrity and will be governed by the Aggie Honor Code'. This describes what the recommended syllabus addition says; it is a statement of fact about governance, not a command, so modality is informs and the stance neutral (B). Actor all (it applies to anyone using AI in coursework), not admin. A's normalized policy text is kept because the anchor alone lacks the subject.
units.anchor: will be governed by the Aggie Honor Code
units.policy: Use of generative AI in academic coursework is integrally related to academic integrity and will be governed by the Aggie Honor Code.
units.fit_note: States that AI use is governed by the Aggie Honor Code but does not itself classify any use as misconduct.

units.why: The hybrid includes "Guidance provided to support faculty in making their individual determinations"; support for faculty deciding AI policy fits P63.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (modality: A=should, B=informs). Source: item 3b of the recommended hybrid, 'Guidance provided to support faculty in making their individual determinations'. It sits under the recommended option, so it is a recommendation (should), not a bare description.
units.anchor: Guidance provided to support faculty in making their individual determinations

units.why: Clarifies that the sample statements are instructors' own syllabus language, not institutional policy; this scopes what the samples mean, closest to P61 (scope).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (actor: A=admin, B=instructor; phase: A=general, B=before-course; policy_type: A=P61, B=P04). Source: 'The samples represent instructor uses on their own syllabi and not institutional policies.' It defines what the samples are, i.e. the scope of what follows, which is P61 with a fit note, not an instructor-discretion rule (P04, B). Actor admin, phase general (A).
units.anchor: The samples represent instructor uses on their own syllabi and not institutional policies.
units.fit_note: Scope note about the status of the samples rather than a definition of AI.

units.why: Sample (Bryant) statement bans AI writing tools "for any stage or phase of work": a default ban on all work, P01.
units.anchor: AI Writing tools are not permitted for any stage or phase of work

units.why: Sample (Bryant): using the tools "would be considered academically dishonest"; classifies prohibited AI use as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: your actions would be considered academically dishonest and a violation of Bryant

units.why: Sample (Princeton): "All work submitted in this course must be your own"; students own what they submit, P29.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=prohibit, B=restrict). Source: Princeton's 'All work submitted in this course must be your own, completed in accordance with the University's academic regulations.' The sentence demands own work but does not itself mention AI (the next sentence bans ChatGPT, coded separately), so unit_stance restrict (B) fits better than prohibit (A). The type P29 and the other fields agree.
units.anchor: All work submitted in this course must be your own

units.why: Sample (Princeton) bars use of ChatGPT or other AI composition software outright: P01.
units.anchor: You may not engage in unauthorized collaboration or make use of ChatGPT

units.why: Sample (Texas Tech): because writing and thinking skills are learning outcomes, "all writing assignments should be prepared by the student"; the student must produce the submitted text, P19.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (policy_type: A=P19, B=P41). Source (Texas Tech sample): 'all writing assignments should be prepared by the student'. The sentence states the rule that submitted writing is the student's own, i.e. do not have AI produce it, P19 (A). P41 (B) fits the following sentence about competence, not this one. Modality stays should as worded.
units.anchor: all writing assignments should be prepared by the student

units.why: Texas Tech sample: "Developing strong competencies in this area will prepare you for a competitive workplace" is a career reason for doing the work unaided, so P94 (not P44, the learn-AI-for-careers argument).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A=course-start, B=general). Source: 'Developing strong competencies in this area will prepare you for a competitive workplace.' It is a rationale, not an expectation set at the start of the course, so phase general (B) rather than course-start (A).
units.anchor: Developing strong competencies in this area will prepare you for a competitive workplace.

units.why: Texas Tech sample: "AI-generated submissions are not permitted and will be treated as plagiarism"; bars submitting AI output, P19.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A=when-misuse, B=during-work; policy_type: A=P36, B=P19). Source (Texas Tech sample): 'AI-generated submissions are not permitted and will be treated as plagiarism.' The sentence holds two rules. A coded the sanction (P36, when-misuse) and B the ban (P19, during-work). Since one unit may hold only one rule, it is split: this unit is the ban (P19, during-work, must-not), and a second unit takes the plagiarism classification (P36, when-misuse). B's fit note is kept.
units.anchor: AI-generated submissions are not permitted
units.frag_end: and will be treated as plagiarism.
units.fit_note: Also classifies the use as plagiarism (P36).

units.why: Second rule in the Texas Tech sample sentence: 'will be treated as plagiarism' classifies AI-generated submissions as misconduct, handled under integrity rules (P36). The student is bound; the phase is when-misuse because the sentence states how a breach is treated.
units.resolution_why: Split from the ban unit above. Coder A coded the whole sentence as one P36 when-misuse unit and coder B as one P19 during-work unit; the sentence holds two rules (the ban and the plagiarism classification), so each gets its own unit. Source: 'AI-generated submissions are not permitted and will be treated as plagiarism.'
units.anchor: will be treated as plagiarism
units.frag_end: and will be treated as plagiarism.

units.why: Sample (UNH): "Unless otherwise specified" AI tools are strictly prohibited "even when properly attributed"; this states the fallback when the instructor specifies nothing, P06.
units.anchor: Unless otherwise specified, the use of Automated Writing Tools
units.policy: Unless otherwise specified, use of automated writing tools including ChatGPT and similar AI tools is strictly prohibited in the course, even when properly attributed.
units.fit_note: Also says attribution does not cure the violation ("even when properly attributed").

units.why: Sample (UNH): use "is considered plagiarism" and handled under existing policy; P36.
units.anchor: The use of automated writing tools is considered plagiarism

units.why: UC Irvine writing-program sample: all submissions "will be generated by the students themselves"; submitted work must be the student's own, P29.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (modality: A=must-not, B=must; policy_type: A=P19, B=P29; unit_stance: A=prohibit, B=restrict). Source (UC Irvine sample): 'work submitted by students ... will be generated by the students themselves'. A coded one unit with a merged policy covering both this expectation and the ChatGPT violation, which breaks the one-rule-per-unit rule. Split: this unit is the own-work expectation (P29, must, restrict, B); the ChatGPT violation is coded as a separate P19 unit (coder B's unit 19). A's merged policy text is dropped.
units.anchor: all other submissions–will be generated by the students themselves

units.why: UC Irvine sample lists as an integrity violation having another person or entity write a substantive portion, including "using artificial intelligence affordances like ChatGPT"; AI may not produce submitted work, P19.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source (UC Irvine sample): the violations list includes 'using artificial intelligence affordances like ChatGPT' (alongside hiring a person or company). A had merged this rule into its P29 unit; kept as its own P19 unit so that the ban on AI-written work is one rule per unit.
units.anchor: using artificial intelligence affordances like ChatGPT
units.fit_note: Frames AI as one more outside party doing the writing and calls it an integrity violation.

units.why: UMass Amherst sample: "Students should not have another person/entity do the writing ... using artificial intelligence tools like ChatGPT"; P19 as a should-not.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source (UMass sample): 'Students should not have another person/entity do the writing of any substantive portion of an assignment for them ... and using artificial intelligence tools like ChatGPT.' Different wording and modality (should-not) from the UC Irvine entry, so it is kept as its own sample statement.
units.anchor: Students should not have another person/entity do the writing of any substantive portion of an

units.why: Sample (Bryant, some circumstances): AI use is allowed only where the instructor says when, where and how, i.e. decided per activity, P04.
units.anchor: You will be informed as to when, where, and how these tools are permitted

units.why: Sample (Bryant): use outside the permission "constitutes a violation"; unauthorized use is misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: Any use outside of this permission constitutes a violation of Bryant

units.why: Second Bryant sample: "AI programs are not a replacement for human creativity, originality, and critical thinking"; AI must not replace the student's thinking, P32.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A=during-work, B=general). Source: 'AI programs are not a replacement for human creativity, originality, and critical thinking.' A general principle, not an instruction for a stage of work: phase general (B), not during-work (A).
units.anchor: AI programs are not a replacement for human creativity, originality, and critical thinking.

units.why: Sample (Bryant): AI may be used "within limited circumstances, and with proper attribution"; permitted with attribution, P24.
units.anchor: within limited circumstances, and with proper attribution, AI programs may be used as a tool
units.fit_note: Also limits use to limited circumstances. | Also grants limited permission as a tool, which P24 does not capture.

units.why: Sample (Princeton, some circumstances): "must obtain permission from me before using AI composition software"; AI is off unless the instructor permits, P01 (ban unless permitted).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (policy_type: A=P01, B=P04). Source (Princeton sample): 'Students must obtain permission from me before using AI composition software'. The rule is a default ban lifted by prior permission, which is what P01 covers; P04 (B) is about letting instructors set the rule, and this sample is already one instructor's rule. P01 with a fit note.
units.anchor: Students must obtain permission from me before using AI composition software
units.fit_note: Ban lifted by instructor permission rather than an absolute ban. | Also works as a fallback rule: no AI without prior permission (P06).

units.why: Princeton sample: using tools without permission "puts your academic integrity at risk"; links unauthorized use to integrity, P36.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source (Princeton sample): 'Using these tools without my permission puts your academic integrity at risk.' It links unpermitted use to integrity, a stated consequence: kept.
units.anchor: Using these tools without my permission puts your academic integrity at risk.

units.why: Sample (UNH): if permitted, AI tools "should be used with caution and proper citation"; citation requirement, P24.
units.anchor: should be used with caution and proper citation

units.why: Sample (UNH): "AI is not a replacement for your own thinking and research"; students stay the primary thinker, P32.
units.anchor: AI is not a replacement for your own thinking and research

units.why: WashU sample grounds rules in trust in "the integrity of work that is submitted for academic credit"; fairness and integrity culture, P95.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source (WashU sample): the opening of the integrity statement grounds the rules in trust in 'the integrity of work that is submitted for academic credit'. It is a stated rationale: kept as informs.
units.anchor: trust one another and to trust the integrity of work that is submitted for academic

units.why: WashU sample: "work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original"; submitted work must be the student's own, P29.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source (WashU sample): 'work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original'. A real requirement that submitted work be original: kept.
units.anchor: work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original

units.why: Sample (WashU): using an AI generator "without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty"; misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty

units.why: Sample (WashU): "If you are unsure ... please contact your instructor"; ask when unsure, P10.
units.anchor: please contact your instructor to discuss the issue

units.why: Colorado sample: "you will be asked to use AI tools to explore how they can be used"; AI use built into the course, P79.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (modality: A=informs, B=must). Source (Colorado sample): 'there are situations and contexts within this course where you will be asked to use AI tools'. It binds students to a required activity, so modality must (B) with require stance; A's informs treats it as a bare fact.
units.anchor: you will be asked to use AI tools to explore how they can be used

units.why: Sample (Colorado): outside designated tasks students "are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content"; discouraged not forbidden, P03.
units.anchor: you are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content

units.why: Sample (Colorado): work using AI "should clearly indicate what work is the student's work and what part is generated by the AI"; disclosure, P24.
units.anchor: Any student work submitted using AI tools should clearly indicate what work

units.why: Colorado sample caps AI-generated share at 25%; "no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI" fits P16 (percentage cap on generated content).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (modality: A=should, B=should-not). Source (Colorado sample): 'no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI'. It is a cap, i.e. a limit phrased negatively, so should-not (B) rather than should (A). P16 is kept with the fit note both coders wrote (the cap covers text, video, audio and images, not only code).
units.anchor: no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI
units.fit_note: Cap covers generated text, video, audio and images, not specifically code. | The sample concerns text, video, audio and images, not specifically code.

units.why: Sample (Colorado): if unclear, "reach out to me for a conversation before submitting"; ask first, P10.
units.anchor: please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work

units.why: Sample (Bryant, broader use): AI tools "are welcome ... provided that you cite when and how you use the tool"; default permit with citation, P02.
units.anchor: AI Writing tools such as ChatGPT are welcome in this class, provided that you cite
units.fit_note: The welcome is conditional on citing when and how the tool is used.

units.why: Bryant sample: "You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool"; the instructor supplies citation help, P24 as the nearest type.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source (Bryant sample): 'You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool'. It commits the instructor to give citation help, a real statement: kept, with B's fit note.
units.anchor: You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool
units.fit_note: Instructor commitment to supply citation examples rather than a student duty.

units.why: The sample attribution language names the tool and model ("GPT-3, OpenAI's large-scale language-generation model"), an example of citation naming the tool; P25.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=neutral, B=permit). Source (Bryant sample): the model attribution sentence 'The author generated this text in part with GPT-3...'. It is example wording, not a rule about whether AI may be used, so neutral (A); the rule to cite is coded separately.
units.anchor: The author generated this text in part with GPT-3
units.fit_note: Names the model only; no prompt or date.

units.why: The Bryant sample attribution says the author "takes ultimate responsibility for the content"; students own what they submit, P29.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=neutral, B=permit). Source: '... takes ultimate responsibility for the content of this publication' is part of the example attribution wording; it states responsibility but takes no position on AI use, so neutral (A).
units.anchor: takes ultimate responsibility for the content of this publication

units.why: UMass sample: "Use of AI tools, including ChatGPT, is permitted in this course for students who wish to use them"; default permit, P02.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source (UMass sample): 'Use of AI tools, including ChatGPT, is permitted in this course for students who wish to use them.' This is the default permission of that sample; A did not code it. Kept.
units.anchor: Use of AI tools, including ChatGPT, is permitted in this course for students who wish

units.why: Sample (UMass Amherst): "students must cite any AI-generated material that informed their work"; cite AI use, P24.
units.anchor: students must cite any AI-generated material that informed their work

units.why: Sample (UMass Amherst): generating content "without proper attribution qualifies as academic dishonesty"; non-disclosure is itself the violation, P28.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=restrict, B=permit). Source (UMass sample): 'Using an AI tool to generate content without proper attribution qualifies as academic dishonesty.' Use is permitted only with attribution, so the sentence narrows the permission: restrict (A), not permit (B).
units.anchor: without proper attribution qualiﬁes as academic dishonesty

units.why: Sample (UMass Amherst, encouraged): students "can choose to use AI tools to help brainstorm"; brainstorming, P15.
units.anchor: You can choose to use AI tools to help brainstorm assignments or projects
units.fit_note: Also allows AI to revise one's own written work (P91).

units.why: Sample (UMass Amherst, encouraged): AI may be used "to revise existing work you have written"; editing support, P91.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. Source (UMass sample): 'or to revise existing work you have written' is a separate permitted use (revising one's own work) from brainstorming. B folded it into its brainstorming unit as a fit note. Kept as its own unit so each permission is counted once.
units.anchor: or to revise existing work you have written

units.why: Sample (UMass Amherst): "I expect you to clearly attribute what text was generated by the AI tool" e.g. a different font colour; marking AI text where used, P24.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=permit, B=encourage). Source (UMass sample): 'you can choose to use AI tools ... I expect you to clearly attribute what text was generated by the AI tool'. The unit is the attribution condition on a permitted use: permit (A). 'Encourage' belongs to the heading, which is coded in the brainstorming unit.
units.anchor: clearly attribute what text was generated by the AI tool
units.fit_note: Marks AI-generated text in place, e.g. different colored font or parenthetical. | Marks AI text at the place it appears (P27 is for code), so P24 is nearest.

units.why: Iowa sample: "Students should indicate how AI tools informed their process and the final product"; process-level disclosure, P24.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source (Iowa sample): 'Students should indicate how AI tools informed their process and the final product'. A process-level disclosure that the UMass sample does not have: kept.
units.anchor: Students should indicate how AI tools informed their process and the final product

units.why: Sample (Iowa): students "should indicate ... how you validated any AI-generated citations, which may be invented by the AI"; verify output, P31.
units.anchor: how you validated any AI-generated citations, which may be invented by the AI

units.why: Iowa sample: "Assignment guidelines will provide additional guidance"; rules set per assignment, P04.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=permit, B=neutral). Source (Iowa sample): 'Assignment guidelines will provide additional guidance as to how these tools might be part of your process'. It is a pointer to assignment-level guidance and takes no position on AI use: neutral (B), not permit (A).
units.anchor: Assignment guidelines will provide additional guidance as to how these tools might be part of

units.why: Sample (Iowa, encouraged): students "are invited to use AI platforms to help prepare for assignments" e.g. brainstorming; P15.
units.anchor: Students are invited to use AI platforms to help prepare for assignments and projects

units.why: Sample (Iowa, encouraged): "welcome you to use AI tools to help revise and edit your work"; editing support, P91.
units.anchor: I also welcome you to use AI tools to help revise and edit your work

units.why: Sample (Iowa): AI-generated essay parts appear in a different colour and the relationship to student work "should be discussed in cover letters"; reflection submitted with work, P26.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=permit, B=encourage). Source (Iowa sample): the relationship between AI-generated sections and student contributions 'should be discussed in cover letters'. It is a condition attached to permitted use, so permit (A), not encourage (B).
units.anchor: the relationship between those sections and student contributions should be discussed in cover letters

documents.unit: Texas A&M AI initiative / Division of Academic Affairs
documents.title: Use Guidelines and Ethics (Teach with AI)
documents.summary: University AI site page giving ethical principles and role-based best practices for faculty, staff and students. For academic work it asks for cited AI use, allows spelling/grammar help but not new text, and leaves course-level rules to faculty.
documents.stance_why: The page says "The faculty should provide clear instructions about permissible AI uses in their courses" and that professors can require AI per syllabus, while setting shared principles; it does not itself fix a stance, so delegates.

units.why: Purpose: guidance on "responsible use of generative AI" while "minimizing risks to academic integrity, privacy and other ethical use considerations"; institution-level framework, P56.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (actor: A=admin, B=all). Source: the page's purpose paragraph, 'recommendations and guidance on the responsible use of generative AI at Texas A & M University'. The guidance addresses the whole university community, so actor all (B) rather than admin (A).
units.anchor: recommendations and guidance on the responsible use of generative AI at Texas A & M

units.why: "Generative AI use ... should adhere to the same ethical principles ... privacy, fairness, transparency, bias, and accountability"; institution-wide principles, P56.
units.anchor: should adhere to the same ethical principles used in other aspects of education

units.why: "We must ensure that we implement algorithms that incorporate fairness measures and conduct routine audits to detect and address prejudices"; auditing AI systems for bias, P98.
units.anchor: conduct routine audits to detect and address prejudices

units.why: "Everyone should ensure the AI systems are transparent and explainable to professors and students"; closest to P103 (people should understand the AI they deal with).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (policy_type: A=P98, B=P103). Source: 'Everyone should ensure the AI systems are transparent and explainable to professors and students, to increase trust and responsibility.' P98 (A) is about documenting, auditing and monitoring systems, which the preceding sentence ('routine audits') already covers. P103 (B) is about telling people they deal with AI and its limits; explainability to users is the nearer fit but only partly, so P103 with a fit note.
units.anchor: AI systems are transparent and explainable to professors and students
units.fit_note: About transparency and explainability of systems, not telling people they face an AI. | Concerns explainability of AI systems to users rather than audit or monitoring.

units.why: Explains that platforms "may collect, store, and process personal data, potentially leading to privacy risks"; data privacy rationale, P50.
units.anchor: these platforms may collect, store, and process personal data

units.why: "Everyone must follow data privacy and security guidelines ... protecting personal and institutional data"; P50.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=neutral, B=restrict). Source: 'Everyone must follow data privacy and security guidelines when using generative AI'. It is a compliance duty that takes no position on whether AI may be used, so neutral (A), not restrict (B).
units.anchor: Everyone must follow data privacy and security guidelines when using generative AI

units.why: "The use of copyrighted materials to train generative AI models must respect these rights"; copyright, P52.
units.anchor: use of copyrighted materials to train generative AI models must respect these rights

units.why: Transparency: "clearly documenting the use of AI-generated content, properly attributing AI-assisted contributions in research and academic work"; disclosure, P24.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (phase: A=general, B=during-work; modality: A=should, B=informs). Source: the Transparency paragraph says 'This includes clearly documenting the use of AI-generated content, properly attributing AI-assisted contributions'. It is a principle with an expectation inside it, worded as a recommendation: should and general (A). B read it as a bare statement (informs, during-work).
units.anchor: properly attributing AI-assisted contributions in research and academic work

units.why: Transparency principle: implementation of AI tools "aligns with the University's policies and broader ethical standards"; compliance with existing policy, P77.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. Source: the Transparency paragraph says implementation must align with 'the University's policies and broader ethical standards'. A real compliance statement: kept.
units.anchor: ensuring that the implementation of such tools aligns with the University

units.why: "users must acknowledge the use of nontrivial AI-generated content and avoid plagiarism"; disclosure with a triviality threshold, P24.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (actor: A=student, B=all). Source: 'users must acknowledge the use of nontrivial AI-generated content and avoid plagiarism'. 'Users' is not limited to students (the surrounding text covers research and academic work), so actor all (B).
units.anchor: users must acknowledge the use of nontrivial AI-generated content and avoid plagiarism
units.fit_note: Threshold: only nontrivial AI-generated content must be acknowledged.

units.why: "properly citing AI-generated content in academic work"; P24.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. Source: 'This includes properly citing AI-generated content in academic work and ensuring that AI-generated content does not violate academic integrity policies.' It restates the acknowledgement duty in the Academic Integrity paragraph with the added duty not to violate integrity policy: kept.
units.anchor: properly citing AI-generated content in academic work

units.why: "It is permissible to use AI for correcting spelling and grammar and for formatting references"; editing permission, P91.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (unit_stance: A=permit, B=restrict). units.why: FAQ 6: staff disclose AI use for tasks affecting decisions or with ethical or legal implications; staff operational use, P76.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (policy_type: A=P76, B=P103). Source: 'Staff should disclose the use of generative AI when it is used for tasks that can impact decisions or have ethical or legal implications.' It is a rule for AI in staff work, P76 (A). P103 (B) is telling people they are interacting with AI, but the audience here is not named. Fit note kept.
units.anchor: Staff should disclose the use of generative AI when it is used for tasks
units.fit_note: Staff disclosure of AI use in their work, not to students. | Staff disclosure of their own AI use, audience unnamed.

units.why: "disclosure is not necessary for minor tasks or when significant edits are made"; exempts minor use, nearest P100.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (modality: A=may, B=informs; policy_type: A=P76, B=P100; unit_stance: A=permit, B=neutral). Source: 'disclosure is not necessary for minor tasks or when significant edits are made to the AI-generated output'. It exempts minor or heavily edited use from the disclosure duty, the nearest type is P100 (B). Modality may and stance permit (A), since it grants an exemption rather than informing.
units.anchor: disclosure is not necessary for minor tasks or when significant edits are made
units.fit_note: Exempts minor tasks and heavily edited output, not named routine features.

units.why: FAQ 7: "professors can require students to use generative AI tools for assignments, but with certain restrictions"; P79.
units.anchor: professors can require students to use generative AI tools

units.why: FAQ 7: professors "should encourage the use of university-approved AI tools"; P92.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. Source (FAQ 7): professors 'should encourage the use of university-approved AI tools'. A real recommendation: kept.
units.anchor: should encourage the use of university-approved AI tools

units.why: "not require students to create accounts with non-university AI tools that require sharing personal information"; nearest P92 (prefer university-approved tools).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed (policy_type: A=P51, B=P92; unit_stance: A=restrict, B=neutral). Source: professors should 'not require students to create accounts with non-university AI tools that require sharing personal information'. The concern is personal data and use of university tools (P92, B), not cost (P51, A). It limits what instructors may require, so restrict (A).
units.anchor: not require students to create accounts with non-university AI tools that require sharing personal information
units.fit_note: Also protects students from sharing personal data through required accounts (P50). | Frames the limit as personal-information sharing, not cost.

units.why: FAQ 8: submitting AI work "as one's own without proper acknowledgment constitutes cheating"; misconduct, P36 (also non-acknowledgment).
units.anchor: as one's own without proper acknowledgment constitutes cheating and violates academic integrity policies
units.fit_note: Also makes nondisclosure the violation (P28).

notes: Reconciled from coder A and coder B. u1 consists mostly of sample syllabus statements borrowed from other universities (stated by the CTE to be instructor samples, not TAMU policy); they are coded as the permission-level examples the CTE endorses. Split into one rule per unit: the Texas Tech 'not permitted ... treated as plagiarism' sentence (ban plus plagiarism classification), the UC Irvine own-work expectation and ChatGPT violation, and the u2 'spelling and grammar permitted, not new text' sentence. Dropped as non-policies or exact repeats: texas-aandm-u1 B unit 3: Coder B only. Option 1 of three courses of action the CTE lists; the document recommends option 3 (the hybrid) and presents options 1 and 2 only as candidates, not as adopted rules. Dropped as not a stated policy. texas-aandm-u1 B unit 4: Coder B only (it had been auto-paired with A3 but covers a different passage). Option 2 of three candidate courses of action, not the recommended one and not an adopted rule. Dropped as not a stated policy. texas-aandm-u1 B unit 22: Coder B only. The Iowa sample repeats the UC Irvine wording word for word (it says it is excerpted from UC Irvine); the same rule is already coded once from the UC Irvine entry. Dropped as an exact repeat. texas-aandm-u1 B unit 49: Coder B only. Third copy of the WashU/Iowa sentence 'without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty', already coded once. Dropped as an exact repeat. texas-aandm-u1 B unit 50: Coder B only. The Iowa sample repeats the UMass sentence 'Use of AI tools, including ChatGPT, is permitted in this course for students who wish to use them' word for word; already coded once. Dropped as an exact repeat. texas-aandm-u1 B unit 51: Coder B only. The Iowa sample repeats the UMass sentence 'students must cite any AI-generated material that informed their work' word for word; already coded once. Dropped as an exact repeat. texas-aandm-u1 B unit 57: Coder B only. Iowa wording of the same marking rule already coded from the UMass sample ('clearly attribute what text was generated by the AI tool'): AI-generated text must be identified. Dropped as a near repeat of an existing unit. In u2, sibling list items that neither coder coded (e.g. two of the four staff 'Enhancing Efficiency' items) were not added. Course layer deferred; no school or computing-unit policy found.
